Pivot (trochoid) synovial joint
Hinge (ginglymus) joint

explanation: Atlanto-axial joint = pivot joint; knee/elbow = hinge joint; shoulder/hip = ball-and-socket joint; carpometacarpal of thumb = saddle joint; intercarpal = gliding joint.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 16: Skeleton and Movement (Synovial Joints Classification)

questionText: Human thoracic cage contains 12 pairs of bicephalic ribs. Why are the 8th, 9th, and 10th pairs designated 'vertebrochondral (false) ribs' whereas the 11th and 12th pairs are 'floating ribs'?

options.text: Pairs 8–10 lack dorsal articulation with thoracic vertebrae, whereas pairs 11–12 fuse with lumbar vertebrae
Pairs 8–10 do not articulate directly with the sternum but join the hyaline cartilage of the 7th rib, whereas pairs 11–12 remain free ventrally
Pairs 8–10 float freely at both ends, whereas pairs 11–12 articulate with the xiphoid process
Pairs 1–7 are cartilaginous throughout, whereas pairs 8–12 are ossified directly to the clavicle

explanation: Pairs 1–7 are true (vertebrosternal) ribs attached dorsally to thoracic vertebrae and ventrally to sternum; pairs 8–10 attach ventrally to the 7th costal cartilage (vertebrochondral); pairs 11–12 are unattached ventrally (vertebral/floating ribs, protecting kidneys).
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 16: Skeleton and Movement (Rib Cage Classification (True, False, Floating))

topic: Role of Ca^2+ and Troponin-Tropomyosin in Cross-Bridge Cycling
questionText: When an action potential travels down T-tubules of a skeletal muscle fibre, Ca^2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum initiates contraction by binding directly to:

options.text: Acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft
Z-line α-actinin to dissolve the I-band
Troponin-C (TnC) subunit on thin actin filaments, shifting tropomyosin to unmask myosin-binding sites on F-actin
Globular heads of myosin (HMM) to hydrolyse ATP into AMP

explanation: At rest, tropomyosin and the troponin complex sterically block myosin-binding sites on actin; Ca^2+ binding to troponin-C triggers a conformational shift pulling tropomyosin aside so energized myosin heads can form cross-bridges.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 16: Skeleton and Movement (Role of Ca^2+ and Troponin-Tropomyosin in Cross-Bridge Cycling)

topic: Sliding Filament Band Changes During Sarcomere Shortening
questionText: According to Huxley's sliding filament theory, when a skeletal muscle sarcomere contracts maximally from rest, specify exactly what happens to the lengths of (i) A-band, (ii) I-band, (iii) H-zone, and (iv) distance between two successive Z-lines:

options.text: A-band remains constant in length, while I-band shortens, H-zone narrows/disappears, and Z–Z distance (sarcomere length) decreases
Both A-band and myosin filaments shorten by 50%, while I-band and H-zone widen
I-band remains constant in length, while A-band shortens and H-zone widens
Neither A-band nor I-band changes length; only tendons shorten

explanation: Neither thick (myosin) nor thin (actin) myofilaments shorten in actual length; thin filaments slide inward over thick filaments toward the M-line. Because A-band equals thick-filament length, A-band stays constant while I-band, H-zone, and Z-to-Z sarcomere length decrease.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 16: Skeleton and Movement (Sliding Filament Band Changes During Sarcomere Shortening)

topic: Rigor Mortis ATP Mechanics and Muscular Disorders
questionText: Why do skeletal muscles stiffen irreversibly several hours after death ('rigor mortis'), and how does 'myasthenia gravis' differ mechanistically from 'tetany'?

options.text: ATP is needed only for cross-bridge attachment and not detachment; tetany is X-linked dystrophin gene mutation
Rigor mortis occurs because excess post-mortem ATP locks tropomyosin; myasthenia gravis is uric acid crystal deposition in joints (gout)
Myasthenia gravis is caused by hypercalcaemia, whereas tetany is autoimmune demyelination

Post-mortem ATP depletion prevents myosin heads from detaching from actin cross-bridges (binding of fresh unhydrolysed ATP is required to break actomyosin bridges); myasthenia gravis is autoimmune destruction/blockade of neuromuscular acetylcholine receptors (weakness/paralysis), whereas tetany is sustained involuntary spasm from low extracellular Ca^2+ (hypocalcaemia)

explanation: During the cross-bridge cycle, Pi/ADP release drives the power stroke, and binding of a NEW ATP molecule to the myosin head is mandatory for detachment from actin; without ATP after death, Ca^2+ leaks in and actomyosin bridges stay locked (rigor mortis). Myasthenia gravis is autoimmune anti-AChR weakness; tetany is hypocalcaemic hyperexcitability spasm.
syllabusReference: MSBSHSE Class 11 Balbharati Syllabus — Ch. 16: Skeleton and Movement (Rigor Mortis ATP Mechanics and Muscular Disorders)
